page.h1: HTS Chapter 30: Pharmaceutical Products — U.S. Exports & Foreign Tariffs

seo.title: U.S. Pharmaceutical Exports & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Medicines (HTS Ch. 30) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: U.S. pharmaceutical exports were $97.82B in 2025. Where they go, what each country charges on U.S. medicines, and which tariffs changed since January 2025.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$97.82B** of pharmaceuticals in 2025, up 3.6% on 2024 — less than half of the $213.82B it imported, but still one of its largest export chapters. Most of it is biologics: vaccines, antibodies and blood products (heading 3002) were **59%** of the total.

For a U.S. exporter, tariffs are rarely the obstacle. The EU, Japan, Canada, the UK and Switzerland — which together take most U.S. medicines — charge **0%** under the WTO zero-for-zero pharmaceutical agreement or a free-trade agreement. The exceptions are **China**, which adds an extra 10% on all U.S. goods on top of its 0–3% normal rate, and **Brazil**, whose normal rates reach 14%. What decides access is the destination's drug approval, covered on the Export markets page.

keyTakeaways: U.S. pharmaceutical exports reached $97.82B in 2025; biologics (3002) are the core of it.
The EU, Japan, Canada, the UK, Switzerland and Mexico (under USMCA) charge nothing on U.S. medicines, and none of them added a tariff since 2025.
China is the only large buyer charging more than in January 2025: an extra 10% on all U.S. goods, down from a 125% peak in April 2025.
Brazil charges up to 14% and has an open reciprocity case against U.S. tariffs, with nothing imposed yet.
classificationNote: The first six digits of a Chapter 30 code are the same in every country (the Harmonized System). Beyond that each country uses its own schedule: the U.S. reports exports under **Schedule B**, and the duty is set by the **destination's** tariff schedule, not the U.S. one. So the HTS rates on the import pages of this report do not apply to exports.
